label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
		There is an absolute constant $C$ such that, for every real Lipschitz function $A$ and every integer $n\ge 1$,
		\[
		\left\|T_{A,n}\right\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R})\to L^2(\mathbb{R})}\le C\left\|A'\right\|_\infty^n .
		\]
		Specifically, one can take $C=\dfrac{K_0}{2\pi}\,C_{2+\sqrt5}\approx 14.11\; C_{2+\sqrt5}$, where $C_M$ is the constant in the Coifman--McIntosh--Meyer (CMM) theorem for graphs with Lipschitz constant $M$ (Definition~\ref{def:CM}) and $K_0\approx 88.63$ is the numerical constant of Lemma~\ref{lem:integral}.
head: environment
name: Main theorem

label: lem:riesz
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:riesz}
		Let $t:C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})\times C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}) \to\mathbb{C}$ be bilinear with $|t(f,g)|\le B\left\|f\right\|_2\left\|g\right\|_2$. Then there is a unique bounded operator $T$ on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ with $\langle Tf,g\rangle=t(f,g)$ and $\left\|T\right\|\le B$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Apply the Riesz representation theorem to $g\mapsto t(f,\bar g)$ and extend by density.
head: environment

label: lem:weak
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:weak}
		Let $K$ be an antisymmetric kernel such that $|K(x,y)|\le B|x-y|^{-1}$. Let $(E_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be a family of increasing sets satisfying $(x,y)\in E_\varepsilon\iff(y,x)\in E_\varepsilon$, whose union is $\{x\neq y\}$. Assume also that $E_\varepsilon\subset\{|x-y|>\eta(\varepsilon)\}$ for some $\eta(\varepsilon)>0$. Then, for $f,g\inC_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$,
		\[
		\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}\iint_{E_\varepsilon}K(x,y)f(y)g(x)\,dx\,dy=\frac12\iint_{\mathbb{R}^2}K(x,y)\,D(x,y)\,dx\,dy ,
		\]
		and the integral on the right converges absolutely.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
On $E_\varepsilon$ the integrand is bounded by $B\eta(\varepsilon)^{-1}|f(y)||g(x)|$, which is integrable. Exchanging the names of $x$ and $y$ and using the symmetry of $E_\varepsilon$ and the antisymmetry of $K$,
		\[
		\iint_{E_\varepsilon}K(x,y)f(y)g(x)=\iint_{E_\varepsilon}K(y,x)f(x)g(y)=-\iint_{E_\varepsilon}K(x,y)f(x)g(y).
		\]
		Averaging the two expressions gives
		\[
		\iint_{E_\varepsilon}K(x,y)f(y)g(x)\,dx\,dy=\frac12\iint_{E_\varepsilon}K(x,y)\,D(x,y)\,dx\,dy.
		\]
		By \eqref{eq:D}, $|KD|\le Bc_{f,g}\mathbf 1_{S\times S}$, which is integrable. Since $E_\varepsilon\uparrow\{x\ne y\}$ and the diagonal has measure zero, the result follows from dominated convergence.
head: environment

label: def:CM
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:CM}
		For $M\ge0$ we set
		\[
		C_M:=\sup\Bigl\{\left\|\mathcal C_{\Gamma,\varepsilon}\right\|_{L^2(\sigma)\to L^2(\sigma)}:\ \Gamma \text{ a rotated Lipschitz graph with constant}\le M,\ \varepsilon>0\Bigr\}.
		\]
		By construction, $M\mapsto C_M$ is non-decreasing.
head: environment

label: thm:CMM
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:CMM}
		For every $M\ge 0$ there is a finite constant $C_M$, depending only on $M$, such that
		\[
		\left\|\mathcal C_{\Gamma,\varepsilon}\right\|_{L^2(\sigma)\to L^2(\sigma)}\leq C_M
		\]
		for every rotated Lipschitz graph $\Gamma$ with constant not surpassing $M$ and every $\varepsilon>0$.
head: environment
name: Coifman--McIntosh--Meyer

label: rem:CMM
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:CMM}
		Three points about this statement are worth making precise.
		\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
			\item[1.] The theorem of \cite{CMM} is stated for the principal-value operator with $dw$ on graphs $\{s+i\varphi(s)\}$, and the bound depends only on $\left\|\varphi'\right\|_\infty$. The above bound, howeverm is uniform over all truncations and it depends on the arclength measure $\sigma$. This, however, is not an issue, since the kernel $1/(z-w)$ restricted to $\Gamma$ is a standard Calderón--Zygmund kernel with respect to $\sigma$, with constants depending only on $M$, so Cotlar's inequality gives the uniform boundedness of the truncations; see \cite{Jo,Da}.
			\item[2.] Moreover, passing from $dw$ to $d\sigma$ does not change norms. If $\tau$ is the unit tangent, then $dw=(1+i\varphi'(s))\,ds =\tau\,d\sigma$, and hence $\int\frac{F(w)}{z-w}d\sigma(w)=\int\frac{(\bar\tau F)(w)}{z-w}dw$, where multiplication by $\bar\tau$ is an isometry of $L^2(\sigma)$.
			\item[3.] A rotation $z\mapsto e^{i\theta}z$ preserves $\sigma$ and multiplies the kernel by $e^{-i\theta}$, so it does not change norms either.
		\end{enumerate}
		The only thing that will be used from the Coifman--McIntosh--Meyer theorem is that the constant $C_{2+\sqrt5}$ is \emph{finite}. No information about how $C_M$ grows with $M$ will be needed.
head: environment

label: lem:cone
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $e^{-i\theta}\gamma=u+iv$. Almost everywhere, $\gamma'(x)=|\gamma'(x)|e^{i\psi(x)}$ with $|\psi(x)-\theta|\le\Theta/2$, whence
		\[
		u'=|\gamma'|\cos(\psi-\theta)\ge m\cos(\Theta/2)>0,\qquad |v'|=|\gamma'||\sin(\psi-\theta)|\le\tan(\Theta/2)\,u' .
		\]
		Integrating the first inequality, $u(x)-u(y)\ge m\cos(\Theta/2)(x-y)$ for $x>y$. Hence $u$ is an increasing continuous function of $\mathbb{R}$ onto $\mathbb{R}$ with Lipschitz inverse, and since $|\gamma(x)-\gamma(y)|\ge|u(x)-u(y)|$ we obtain \textit{i}). Let $\varphi=v\circ u^{-1}$. For $s=u(x)$ and $s'=u(x')$,
		\[
		|\varphi(s)-\varphi(s')|=\Bigl|\int_{x'}^{x}v'\Bigr|\le\tan(\Theta/2)\Bigl|\int_{x'}^{x}u'\Bigr|=\tan(\Theta/2)\,|s-s'| ,
		\]
		and $\Gamma=e^{i\theta}\{u(x)+iv(x)\}=e^{i\theta}\{s+i\varphi(s)\}$, which proves \textit{ii}). For \textit{iii}), recall that the arclength of the graph is $\sqrt{1+\varphi'(s)^2}\,ds$. Since $u$ is bi-Lipschitz, we may change variables $s=u(x)$, which turns it into
		\[
		\sqrt{1+\varphi'(u(x))^2}\;u'(x)\,dx .
		\]
		By the chain rule, almost everywhere $\varphi'(u(x))=v'(x)/u'(x)$, and then
		\[
		\sqrt{1+\varphi'(u(x))^2}\;u'(x)\,=\,\sqrt{u'(x)^2+v'(x)^2}=|\gamma'(x)| .\qedhere
		\]
head: environment

label: lem:angle
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $\lambda+1=-c(\lambda-1)$ with $c>0$, solving gives $\lambda=\frac{c-1}{c+1}\in(-1,1)$, which is impossible. So the vectors are not opposite, and they are clearly non-zero.
		
		Regarding \textit{i}), observe that the closed sector generated by two vectors forming an angle less than $\pi$ is convex and has opening equal to that angle. Moreover $\lambda-a=\frac{1+a}{2}(\lambda-1)+\frac{1-a}{2}(\lambda+1)$ is a convex combination of the two, so \textit{i}) follows. 
		
		For \textit{ii}), recall if $\alpha$ denotes the the angle between two complex numbers $z_1,z_2$, then
		\[
		\cos{\alpha} = \frac{\operatorname{Re}(z_1\overline{z_2})}{|z_1||z_2|}.
		\]
		Therefore, since $\operatorname{Re}\bigl((\lambda-1)\overline{(\lambda+1)}\bigr)=|\lambda|^2-1+\operatorname{Re}(\lambda-\bar\lambda)=|\lambda|^2-1$, we are done. 
		
		Note also that the maps $\lambda\mapsto\bar\lambda$ and $\lambda\mapsto-\bar\lambda$ are isometries that leave the set $[-1,1]$ invariant (the second one swaps its endpoints), so they preserve the angle under which the segment is seen and thus \textit{iii}) follows. 
		
		Finally, if $\operatorname{Im}\lambda>0$, both vectors lie in the open upper half-plane. Since $\lambda-1=(\lambda+1)-2$, the vector $\lambda-1$ has the larger argument, and the angle between them is the difference of the arguments. The case $\operatorname{Im}\lambda=0$, that is, $\lambda$ real with $|\lambda|>1$, is immediate.
head: environment

label: lem:holo
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:holo}
		The integral \eqref{eq:rlambda} converges absolutely, and $\lambda\mapsto r_\lambda(f,g)$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb{C}\setminus[-1,1]$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By \eqref{eq:D} and \eqref{eq:boundK}, if $\lambda$ ranges over a compact set $F\subset\mathbb{C}\setminus[-1,1]$, the integrand is bounded by $c_{f,g}\,(2\operatorname{dist}(F,[-1,1]))^{-1}\mathbf 1_{S\times S}$. For each $(x,y)$ with $x\neq y$, the function $\lambda\mapsto K_\lambda(x,y)$ is holomorphic. Dominated convergence gives continuity of $\lambda\mapsto r_\lambda(f,g)$, so by Morera's theorem together with Fubini we deduce the holomorphy.
head: environment

label: prop:Rlambda
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:Rlambda}
		For $\lambda\notin[-1,1]$ and $f,g\inC_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$,
		\[
		|r_\lambda(f,g)|\le\frac{C_{M(\lambda)}}{d_\lambda}\,\left\|f\right\|_2\left\|g\right\|_2 .
		\]
		Consequently, by Lemma~\ref{lem:riesz}, $r_\lambda$ is the bilinear form of a bounded operator $R_\lambda$ on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ with $\left\|R_\lambda\right\|\le C_{M(\lambda)}/d_\lambda$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\gamma=\gamma_\lambda$ and $J(x)=|\gamma'(x)|=|\lambda-A'(x)|$. Since $A'(x)\in[-1,1]$ almost everywhere, $J\ge d_\lambda$ almost everywhere.
		
		Since $\gamma'(x)=\lambda-A'(x)$ lies in the segment $\{\lambda-a:a\in[-1,1]\}$, Lemma~\ref{lem:angle} \textit{i}) allows us to apply Lemma~\ref{lem:cone} with $\Theta=\omega(\lambda)$ and $m=d_\lambda$. Thus $\Gamma:=\gamma(\mathbb{R})$ is a rotated Lipschitz graph with constant $\le M(\lambda)$, the map $\gamma$ is injective, and $d\sigma(\gamma(x))=J(x)\,dx$.
		
		Let $E_\varepsilon=\{(x,y):|\gamma(x)-\gamma(y)|>\varepsilon\}$. This family is symmetric, increases as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, and, by injectivity of $\gamma$, its union is $\{x\ne y\}$. Moreover, since $|\gamma(x)-\gamma(y)|\le(|\lambda|+1)|x-y|$, we have $E_\varepsilon\subset\{|x-y|>\varepsilon/(|\lambda|+1)\}$. Lemma~\ref{lem:weak} then gives
		\[
		r_\lambda(f,g)=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}\iint_{E_\varepsilon}\frac{f(y)\,g(x)}{\gamma(x)-\gamma(y)}\,dx\,dy .
		\]
		
		Define the functions $F$ and $G$ on $\Gamma$, $\sigma$-almost everywhere, by
		\[
		F(\gamma(y))=\frac{f(y)}{J(y)},\qquad G(\gamma(x))=\frac{g(x)}{J(x)} .
		\] 
		By Lemma~\ref{lem:cone} \textit{iii}), $F(w)\,d\sigma(w)=f(y)\,dy$ and $G(z)\,d\sigma(z)=g(x)\,dx$. Hence
		\[
		\iint_{E_\varepsilon}\frac{f(y)g(x)}{\gamma(x)-\gamma(y)}\,dx\,dy=\int_\Gamma G(z)\bigg(\int_{|z-w|>\varepsilon}\frac{F(w)}{z-w}\,d\sigma(w)\bigg)\,d\sigma(z)=\int_\Gamma G\;\mathcal C_{\Gamma,\varepsilon}F\,d\sigma .
		\]
		Fubini is justified because $|z-w|>\varepsilon$ and $F,G$ are integrable with compact support.
		
		Finally, by Cauchy--Schwarz and Definition~\ref{def:CM},
		\[
		\Bigl|\int_\Gamma G\,\mathcal C_{\Gamma,\varepsilon}F\,d\sigma\Bigr|\le C_{M(\lambda)}\left\|F\right\|_{L^2(\sigma)}\left\|G\right\|_{L^2(\sigma)} .
		\]
		Finally,
		\[
		\left\|F\right\|_{L^2(\sigma)}^2=\int_\mathbb{R}\frac{|f(y)|^2}{J(y)^2}\,J(y)\,dy=\int_\mathbb{R}\frac{|f|^2}{J}\le\frac{\left\|f\right\|_2^2}{d_\lambda},
		\]
		and the same holds for $G$. Letting $\varepsilon\to0$ gives the bound.
head: environment

label: lem:coef
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:coef}
		Let $\Gamma$ be a piecewise $C^1$ Jordan curve contained in $\mathbb{C}\setminus[-1,1]$, positively oriented, with $[-1,1]$ in its interior. Then, for $f,g\inC_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$,
		\[
		t_n(f,g)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma\lambda^n\,r_\lambda(f,g)\,d\lambda .
		\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $d_\Gamma=\operatorname{dist}(\Gamma,[-1,1])$, which is positive by compactness. The function
		\[
		\Phi(\lambda,x,y)=\lambda^n\,\frac{D(x,y)}{2(x-y)(\lambda-q(x,y))}
		\]
		satisfies $|\Phi|\le|\lambda|^n\,c_{f,g}(2d_\Gamma)^{-1}\mathbf 1_{S\times S}(x,y)$, which is integrable with respect to $|d\lambda|\,dx\,dy$ on $\Gamma\times\mathbb{R}^2$. Fubini allows us to exchange the integrals. For fixed $x\ne y$, the number $q=q(x,y)$ lies inside $\Gamma$, and the Cauchy integral formula gives 
		\[
		\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma\frac{\lambda^n}{\lambda-q}\,d\lambda=q^n.
		\]
		Therefore
		\[
		\frac1{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma\lambda^nr_\lambda(f,g)\,d\lambda=\frac12\iint\frac{q(x,y)^n}{x-y}\,D(x,y)\,dx\,dy=t_n(f,g).\qedhere
		\]
head: environment

label: cor:principle
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:principle}
		For every curve $\Gamma$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem:coef},
		\[
		\left\|T_{A,n}\right\|\le\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_\Gamma|\lambda|^n\,\frac{C_{M(\lambda)}}{d_\lambda}\,|d\lambda|\le\frac{C_{M_\Gamma}}{2\pi}\,I_n(\Gamma),
		\]
		where $M_\Gamma:=\sup_{\lambda\in\Gamma}M(\lambda)$ and $I_n(\Gamma):=\displaystyle\int_\Gamma\frac{|\lambda|^n}{d_\lambda}\,|d\lambda|$.
head: environment

label: prop:log
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:log}
		For $n\ge1$ we have $\left\|T_{A,n}\right\|\le 2e\,C_1\,(1+\log n)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Take $\Gamma=\{|\lambda|=\rho\}$ with $\rho=1+\frac1n$. Since $|\lambda|>1$, Lemma~\ref{lem:angle} \textit{ii}) gives $\omega(\lambda)<\pi/2$. Hence $M(\lambda)\le\tan(\pi/4)=1$ and $M_\Gamma\le1$.
		
		Since $[-1,1]$ is contained in the closed unit disc, $d_\lambda\ge\rho-1=\frac1n$. Since it is also contained in $\mathbb{R}$, writing $\lambda=\rho e^{i\theta}$ it is also clear that $d_\lambda\ge|\operatorname{Im}\lambda|=\rho|\sin\theta|\ge|\sin\theta|$. Using $\sin\theta\ge2\theta/\pi$ on $[0,\pi/2]$ and symmetry,
		\[
		\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{\max(\frac1n,|\sin\theta|)}\le4\Bigl(\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2n}}n\,d\theta+\int_{\frac{\pi}{2n}}^{\frac\pi2}\frac{\pi}{2\theta}\,d\theta\Bigr)=2\pi(1+\log n).
		\]
		Since $|\lambda|^n=(1+\frac1n)^n\le e$ and $|d\lambda|=\rho\,d\theta\le2\,d\theta$, we get $I_n(\Gamma)\le4\pi e(1+\log n)$. Corollary~\ref{cor:principle} concludes.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
On the circle, $|\lambda|^n$ does not decay anywhere, and near $\pm1$ the integral of $1/d_\lambda$ produces $\log n$. To remove it one has to pass \emph{inside} the unit disc, where $|\lambda|^n$ decays exponentially at scale $1/n$. The price is that there $\omega(\lambda)>\pi/2$, and if $\lambda$ approaches the segment tangentially, then $\omega(\lambda)\to\pi$ and $M(\lambda)\to\infty$. The solution is to reach $\pm1$ at a fixed angle to the segment.
		
		Near $\lambda=1$, along a ray $\lambda=1+s e^{i(\pi-\varphi)}$, we have $|\lambda|^n\approx e^{-ns\cos\varphi}$ and $d_\lambda\approx s\sin\varphi$. The integral
		\[
		\int_{1/n}^{1}\frac{e^{-cns}}{s}\,ds=\int_1^n\frac{e^{-cu}}{u}\,du
		\]
		is bounded uniformly in $n$ by scale invariance. This is the mechanism of Section~\ref{sec:contour}.
head: environment

label: def:contour
title: Definition
head: environment
name: The contour

label: lem:jordan
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:jordan}
		$\Gamma_\delta$ is a Jordan curve contained in $\mathbb{C}\setminus[-1,1]$, positively oriented, with $[-1,1]$ in its interior.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The upper half $\Gamma^+$, formed by the part of $\mathcal A_R$ with $t\in[0,\pi-\varphi]$, the sides $\Sigma_R^+$ and $\Sigma_L^+$, and the part of $\mathcal A_L$ with $t\in[\varphi,\pi]$, runs from $1+\delta$ to $-1-\delta$ with strictly decreasing real part. Indeed, on the arcs the real part is $\pm1+\delta\cos t$, which is monotone on those intervals, and on the sides it is affine in $s$. Hence $\Gamma^+$ is the graph of a continuous function $h$ on $[-1-\delta,1+\delta]$, positive in the interior of the interval and vanishing at its endpoints. The lower half is the conjugate, that is, the graph of $-h$. Consequently, $\Gamma_\delta$ is the boundary of the domain $\{a+ib:|a|<1+\delta,\ |b|<h(a)\}$, which contains $[-1,1]$. The orientation is positive because $\Gamma^+$ is traversed from right to left. Finally, $\Gamma_\delta$ does not meet $[-1,1]$: on the sides $|\operatorname{Im}\lambda|=\frac s2\ge\frac{s_\delta}2>0$, and the arcs touch the real axis only at $\pm(1+\delta)$.
head: environment

label: lem:angular
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:angular}
		For every $\delta\in(0,\frac12]$ and every $\lambda\in\Gamma_\delta$ we have $\omega(\lambda)\le\pi-\varphi$. Consequently, $M_{\Gamma_\delta}\le M_0=2+\sqrt5$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:angle} \textit{iii}), it suffices to consider $\Sigma_R^+$ and the upper half of $\mathcal A_R$. Indeed, conjugation maps the lower pieces onto the upper ones, and $\lambda\mapsto-\bar\lambda$ maps $\Sigma_R^+$ onto $\Sigma_L^+$ and $\mathcal A_R$ onto $\mathcal A_L$. We use the formula in Lemma~\ref{lem:angle} \textit{iv}).
		
		\emph{Side $\Sigma_R^+$.} We have $\lambda-1=s(-1+\frac i2)$, whose argument is $\pi-\varphi$, and $\lambda+1=2-s+\frac i2 s$, whose argument is $\arctan\frac{s}{2(2-s)}$. This function is increasing in $s\in[0,1]$ and equals $\arctan\frac12=\varphi$ at $s=1$, so the argument of $\lambda+1$ lies in $[0,\varphi]$. Hence $\omega(\lambda)\in[\pi-2\varphi,\pi-\varphi]$.
		
		\emph{Arc $\mathcal A_R$, with $t\in[0,\pi-\varphi]$.} The argument of $\lambda-1=\delta e^{it}$ is $t$. The vectors $2$ and $\delta e^{it}$ lie in the convex sector $\{\arg\in[0,t]\}$, because $t<\pi$, and therefore so does their sum $\lambda+1=2+\delta e^{it}$. So the argument of $\lambda+1$ lies in $[0,t]$ and $\omega(\lambda)\le t\le\pi-\varphi$. The last assertion follows because $\tan$ is increasing on $[0,\pi/2)$.
head: environment

label: lem:integral
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:integral}
		For $n\ge1$ and $\delta=\frac1{n+1}$,
		\[
		I_n(\Gamma_\delta)=\int_{\Gamma_\delta}\frac{|\lambda|^n}{d_\lambda}\,|d\lambda|\le K_0:=4\pi\sqrt5\,e+4\sqrt5\,E_1\!\Bigl(\frac{3}{8\sqrt5}\Bigr)\approx 88.63,
		\]
		where $E_1(a)=\int_a^\infty e^{-v}v^{-1}\,dv$ is the exponential integral.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Arcs.} Let $\lambda=1+\delta e^{it}\in\mathcal A_R$. If $\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge1$, the closest point of $[-1,1]$ is $1$, and $d_\lambda=\delta$. If $\operatorname{Re}\lambda<1$, then $\cos t<0$, that is, $|t|\in(\pi/2,\pi-\varphi]$, and $\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge1-\delta\ge\frac12$. In that case the closest point is the real projection, and
		\[
		d_\lambda=\delta|\sin t|\ge\delta\sin(\pi-\varphi)=\frac{\delta}{\sqrt5},
		\]
		because $\sin$ is decreasing on $[\pi/2,\pi]$. In both cases $d_\lambda\ge\delta/\sqrt5$. Moreover $|\lambda|^n\le(1+\delta)^n\le e^{n/(n+1)}<e$, and the length of the arc is $2(\pi-\varphi)\delta<2\pi\delta$. The contribution of $\mathcal A_R$ is therefore less than $2\pi\delta\cdot e\sqrt5/\delta=2\pi\sqrt5\,e$. The same holds for $\mathcal A_L$, by the symmetry $\lambda\mapsto-\bar\lambda$, which preserves $|\lambda|$ and $d_\lambda$.
		
		\emph{Sides.} On $\Sigma_R^+$, $\operatorname{Re}\lambda=1-s\in[0,1)$, so $d_\lambda=|\operatorname{Im}\lambda|=\frac s2$, and $|d\lambda|=|-1+\frac i2|\,ds=\frac{\sqrt5}2\,ds$. Moreover, for $0\le s\le1$,
		\[
		|\lambda|^2=(1-s)^2+\frac{s^2}{4}=1-2s+\frac54s^2\le1-\frac34s ,
		\]
		because $\frac54s^2\le\frac54s$. Hence $|\lambda|^n\le(1-\frac34s)^{n/2}\le e^{-3ns/8}$. The contribution of $\Sigma_R^+$ is therefore at most
		\[
		\int_{s_\delta}^1e^{-3ns/8}\,\frac{2}{s}\,\frac{\sqrt5}{2}\,ds=\sqrt5\int_{ns_\delta}^{n}\frac{e^{-3u/8}}{u}\,du\le\sqrt5\int_{1/\sqrt5}^\infty\frac{e^{-3u/8}}{u}\,du=\sqrt5\,E_1\!\Bigl(\frac{3}{8\sqrt5}\Bigr),
		\]
		where we used $ns_\delta=\frac{2n}{\sqrt5(n+1)}\ge\frac{1}{\sqrt5}$ for $n\ge1$. The other three sides have the same $|\lambda|$ and the same $d_\lambda$ as functions of $s$: for $\Sigma_L^\pm$, $|\lambda|^2=(1-s)^2+\frac{s^2}4$ and $\operatorname{Re}\lambda=-1+s\in(-1,0]$. Hence they satisfy the same bound. Adding the six contributions gives $K_0$. Numerically, $E_1(3/(8\sqrt5))\approx1.3693$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume first $\left\|A'\right\|_\infty\le1$, let $n\ge1$ and take $\delta=\frac1{n+1}\le\frac12$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:jordan}, $\Gamma_\delta$ satisfies the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:coef}. Corollary~\ref{cor:principle}, together with Lemmas~\ref{lem:angular} and~\ref{lem:integral}, gives
		\[
		\left\|T_{A,n}\right\|\le\frac{C_{M_0}}{2\pi}\,I_n(\Gamma_\delta)\le\frac{K_0}{2\pi}\,C_{2+\sqrt5}\approx14.11\,C_{2+\sqrt5},
		\]
		and this constant is finite by Theorem~\ref{thm:CMM}. For general $A$ with $L=\left\|A'\right\|_\infty>0$ we apply the above to $A/L$ and use $T_{A,n}=L^nT_{A/L,n}$. The case $L=0$ is trivial.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Let $A(x)=Lx+b$ with $L>0$. All secant slopes equal $L$, and therefore $T_{A,n}=L^nH_0$, with $H_0f=\operatorname{p.v.}\int\frac{f(y)}{x-y}\,dy$. With the convention $\hat f(\xi)=\int e^{-ix\xi}f(x)\,dx$, the multiplier of $H_0$ is $-i\pi\operatorname{sgn}\xi$, so $\left\|T_{A,n}\right\|=\pi L^n$. Setting
		\[
		c_n:=\sup_{A}\frac{\left\|T_{A,n}\right\|}{\left\|A'\right\|_\infty^n},
		\]
		we have $\pi\le c_n\le14.11\,C_{2+\sqrt5}$ for every $n$. With the kernels normalised by $1/\pi$, the lower bound is $1$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: Only the finiteness of $C_{M_0}$ for the fixed value $M_0=2+\sqrt5$ is used. The growth of $C_M$ with $M$, such as David's linear bound, plays no role. The value $\varphi=\arctan\frac12$ is not special. Any angle $\varphi\in(0,\pi/4)$ works with minor changes: the straight sides have slope $\tan\varphi$, meet on the imaginary axis and satisfy $|\lambda|^2\le1-cs$. In exchange, $M_0=\cot(\varphi/2)$ and $K_0$ then depend on $\varphi$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: The proof uses the Coifman–McIntosh–Meyer theorem as an input and does not provide an independent proof of that theorem. Its quantitative content is that boundedness of the Cauchy integral on graphs with the single fixed Lipschitz constant $M_0=2+\sqrt5$, combined with the contours constructed in Section \ref{sec:contour}, yields a bound for $T_{A,n}$ that is uniform in $n$. No information about the growth of $C_M$ as $M\to\infty$ is used.

body_md: The theorem concerns the principal-value operator, that is, the form $t_n$. We do not discuss quantitative bounds for the truncations or for the maximal truncation operator in these text.
